entries.604f857cdde354185d6e126c5f920d2d2d6ac5b8: <div sID="gen20951" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Zech.11" sID="Zech.11"/> <div eID="gen20951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20952" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20953" type="x-p"/> God's prophet, who, in the chapters before, was an ambassador sent to promise peace, is here a herald sent to declare war. The Jewish nation shall recover its prosperity, and shall flourish for some time and become considerable; it shall be very happy, at length, in the coming of the long-expected Messiah, in the preaching of his gospel, and in the setting up of his standard there. But, when thereby the chosen remnant among them are effectually called in and united to Christ, the body of the nation, persisting in unbelief, shall be utterly abandoned and given up to ruin, for rejecting Christ; and it is this that is foretold here in this chapter—the Jews rejecting Christ, which was their measure-filling sin, and the wrath which for that sin came upon them to the uttermost. Here is, I. A prediction of the destruction itself that should come upon the Jewish nation, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.1-Zech.11.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The putting of it into the hands of the Messiah. 1. He is charged with the custody of that flock, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.4-Zech.11.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. 2. He undertakes it, and bears rule in it, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7-Zech.11.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. 3. Finding it perverse, he gives it up (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.9">ver. 9</reference>), breaks his shepherd's staff (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10-Zech.11.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>), resents the indignities done him and the contempt put upon him (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12-Zech.11.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>), and then breaks his other staff, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">ver. 14</reference>. 4. He turns them over into the hands of foolish shepherds, who, instead of preventing, shall complete their ruin, and both the blind leaders and the blind followers shall fall together into the ditch, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.15-Zech.11.17">ver. 15-17</reference>. This is foretold to the poor of the flock before it comes to pass, that, when it does come to pass, they may not be offended.
entries.9cb3e26f806fd174fe4b7cd0f68f042ebf9f7934: <div eID="gen20953" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20952" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction of the Jewish State. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20954" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Open thy doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour thy cedars. <hi type="super">2</hi> Howl, fir tree; for the cedar is fallen; because the mighty are spoiled: howl, O ye oaks of Bashan; for the forest of the vintage is come down. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a voice of the howling of the shepherds; for their glory is spoiled: a voice of the roaring of young lions; for the pride of Jordan is spoiled. <div eID="gen20954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20955" type="x-p"/> In dark and figurative expressions, as is usual in the scripture predictions of things at a great distance, that destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish church and nation is here foretold which our Lord Jesus, when the time was at hand, prophesied of very plainly and expressly. We have here, 1. Preparation made for that destruction (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Open thy doors, O Lebanon!</hi> Thou wouldst not open them to let thy king in—he <hi type="italic">came to his own and his own received him not;</hi> now thou must open them to let thy ruin in. Let the gates of the forest, and all the avenues to it, be thrown open, and let the fire come in and devour its glory." Some by Lebanon here understand the temple, which was built of cedars from Lebanon, and the stones of it white as the snow of Lebanon. It was burnt with fire by the Romans, and its gates were forced open by the fury of the soldiers. To confirm this, they tell a story, that forty years before the destruction of the second temple the gates of it opened of their own accord, upon which prodigy Rabbi Johanan made this remark (as it is found in one of the Jewish authors), "Now I know," said he, "that the destruction of the temple is at hand, according to the prophecy of Zechariah, <hi type="italic">Open thy doors, O Lebanon! that the fire may devour thy cedars.</hi>" Others understand it of Jerusalem, or rather of the whole land of Canaan, to which Lebanon was an inlet on the north. All shall lie open to the invader, and the cedars, the mighty and eminent men, shall be devoured, which cannot but alarm those of an inferior rank, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.2">v. 2</reference>. If <hi type="italic">the cedars</hi> have <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> (if <hi type="italic">all the mighty are spoiled,</hi> and brought to ruin), let the <hi type="italic">fir-tree howl.</hi> How can the slender fir-trees stand if stately cedars fall? If cedars are devoured by fire, it is time for the fir-trees to howl; for no wood is so combustible as that of the fir. And let the <hi type="italic">oaks of Bashan,</hi> that lie exposed to every injury, <hi type="italic">howl, for the forest of the vintage</hi> (or the <hi type="italic">flourishing vineyard,</hi> that used to be guarded with a particular care) has come down, or (as some read it) when the <hi type="italic">defenced forests,</hi> such as Lebanon was, have come down. Note, The falls of the wise and good into sin, and the falls of the rich and great into trouble, are loud alarms to those that are every way their inferiors not to be secure. 2. Lamentation made for the destruction (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is a voice of howling.</hi> Those who have fallen howl for grief and shame, and those who see their own turn coming howl for fear. But the great men especially receive the alarm with the utmost confusion. Those who were roaring in the day of their revels and triumphs are howling in the day of their terrors; <hi type="italic">for now they are tormented</hi> more than others. Those great men were by office shepherds, and such should have protected God's flock committed to their charge; it is the duty both of princes and priests. But they were as <hi type="italic">young lions,</hi> that made themselves a terror to the flock with their roaring and the flock a prey to themselves with their tearing. Note, It is sad with a people when those who should be as shepherds to them are as young lions to them. But what is the issue? The shepherds <hi type="italic">howl,</hi> for <hi type="italic">their glory is spoiled.</hi> Their pastures, and the flocks which covered them, which were the glory of the swains, are laid waste. The <hi type="italic">young lions howl,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the pride of Jordan is spoiled.</hi> The pride of Jordan was the thickets on the banks, in which the lions reposed themselves; and therefore, when the river overflowed and spoiled them, the lions came up from them (as we read <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer. xlix. 19</reference>), and they came up roaring. Note, When those who have power proudly abuse their power, and, instead of being shepherds, are as young lions, they may expect that the righteous God will humble their pride and break their power.
entries.0c83b0f8943f1f4dd0f931dee7c74193d938e2ed: <div eID="gen20955" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted and Typified. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20956" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God; Feed the flock of the slaughter; <hi type="super">5</hi> Whose possessors slay them, and hold themselves not guilty: and they that sell them say, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for I am rich: and their own shepherds pity them not. <hi type="super">6</hi> For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but, lo, I will deliver the men every one into his neighbour's hand, and into the hand of his king: and they shall smite the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will feed the flock of slaughter, <hi type="italic">even</hi> you, O poor of the flock. And I took unto me two staves; the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Bands; and I fed the flock. <hi type="super">8</hi> Three shepherds also I cut off in one month; and my soul loathed them, and their soul also abhorred me. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then said I, I will not feed you: that that dieth, let it die; and that that is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let the rest eat every one the flesh of another. <hi type="super">10</hi> And I took my staff, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Beauty, and cut it asunder, that I might break my covenant which I had made with all the people. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it was broken in that day: and so the poor of the flock that waited upon me knew that it <hi type="italic">was</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> And I said unto them, If ye think good, give <hi type="italic">me</hi> my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty <hi type="italic">pieces</hi> of silver. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty <hi type="italic">pieces</hi> of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> Then I cut asunder mine other staff, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Bands, that I might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. <div eID="gen20956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20957" type="x-p"/> The prophet here is made a type of Christ, as the prophet Isaiah sometimes was; and the scope of these verses is to show that <hi type="italic">for judgment Christ came into this world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">John ix. 39</reference>), for judgment to the Jewish church and nation, which were, about the time of his coming, wretchedly corrupted and degenerated by the worldliness and hypocrisy of their rulers. Christ would have healed them, but they would not be healed; they are therefore left desolate, and abandoned to ruin. Observe here, <div eID="gen20957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20958" type="x-p"/> I. The desperate case of the Jewish church, under the tyranny of their own governors. Their slavery in their own country made them as miserable as their captivity in strange countries had done: <hi type="italic">Their possessors slay them and sell them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">v. 5</reference>. In Zechariah's time we find the rulers and the nobles justly rebuked for <hi type="italic">exacting usury of their brethren;</hi> and the governors, even by their servants, oppressive to the people, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.7">Neh. v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">15</reference>. In Christ's time the <hi type="italic">chief priests</hi> and the <hi type="italic">elders,</hi> who were the possessors of the flock, by their traditions, the commandments of men, and their impositions on the consciences of the people, became perfect tyrants, devoured their houses, engrossed their wealth, and fleeced the flock instead of feeding it. The Sadducees, who were deists, corrupted their judgments. The Pharisees, who were bigots for superstition, corrupted their morals, by making void the commandments of God, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.16">Matt. xv. 16</reference>. Thus they slew the sheep of the flock, thus they sold them. They cared not what became of them so they could but gain their own ends and serve their own interests. And, 1. In this they justified themselves: They <hi type="italic">slay them</hi> and <hi type="italic">hold themselves not guilty.</hi> They think that there is no harm in it, and that they shall never be called to an account for it by the chief Shepherd; as if their power were given them for destruction, which was designed only for edification, and as if, because they sat in Moses's seat, they were not under the obligation of Moses's law, but might dispense with it, and with themselves in the breach of it, at their pleasure. Note, Those have their minds woefully blinded indeed who do ill and justify themselves in doing it; but God will not hold those guiltless who hold themselves so. 2. In this they affronted God, by giving him thanks for the gain of their oppression: They said, <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord, for I am rich,</hi> as if, because they prospered in their wickedness, got money by it, and raised estates, God had made himself patron of their unjust practices, and Providence had become <hi type="italic">particeps criminis—the associate of their guilt.</hi> What is got honestly we ought to give God thanks for, and to bless him whose blessing <hi type="italic">makes rich and adds no sorrow with it.</hi> But with what face can we go to God either to beg a blessing upon the unlawful methods of getting wealth or to return him thanks for success in them? They should rather have gone to God to confess the sin, to take shame to themselves for it, and to vow restitution, than thus to mock him by making the gains of sin the gift of God, who <hi type="italic">hates robbery for burnt-offerings,</hi> and reckons not himself praised by the thanksgiving if he be dishonoured either in the getting or the using of that which we give him thanks for. 3. In this they put contempt upon the people of God, as unworthy their regard or compassionate consideration: <hi type="italic">Their own shepherds pity them not;</hi> they make them miserable, and then do not commiserate them. Christ had <hi type="italic">compassion on the multitude because they fainted and were scattered abroad, as if they had no shepherd</hi> (as really they had worse than none); but <hi type="italic">their own shepherds pitied them not,</hi> nor showed any concern for them. Note, It is ill for a church when its pastors have no tenderness, no compassion for precious souls, when they can look upon the ignorant, the foolish, the wicked, the weak, without pity. <div eID="gen20958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20959" type="x-p"/> II. The sentence of God's wrath passed upon them for their senselessness and stupidity in this condition. There was a general decay, nay, a destruction, of religion among them, and it was all one to them; they regarded it not. <hi type="italic">My people love to have it so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jer. v. 31</reference>. Though they were <hi type="italic">oppressed and broken in judgment,</hi> yet they <hi type="italic">willingly walked after the commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.11">Hos. v. 11</reference>. And, as their shepherds pitied them not, so they did not bemoan themselves; therefore God says (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.6">v. 6</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land.</hi> They have courted their own destruction, and so let their doom be." But those are truly miserable whom the God of mercy himself will no more have compassion upon. Those who are willing to have their consciences oppressed by those who <hi type="italic">teach for doctrines the commandments of men</hi> (as the Jews were, who called those <hi type="italic">Rabbi, Rabbi,</hi> that did so, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.9">Matt. xv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.7">xxiii. 7</reference>), are often punished by oppression in their civil interests, and justly, for those forfeit their own rights who tamely give up God's rights. The Jews did so; the Papists do so; and who can pity them if they be ruled with rigour? God here threatens them, 1. That he will deliver them into the hand of oppressors, <hi type="italic">every one into his neighbour's hand,</hi> so that they shall use one another barbarously. The several parties in Jerusalem did so; the <hi type="italic">zealots,</hi> the <hi type="italic">seditious,</hi> as they were called, committed greater outrages than the common enemy did, as Josephus relates in his history of the wars of the Jews. They shall be delivered every one <hi type="italic">into the hand of his king,</hi> that is, the Roman emperor, whom they chose to submit to rather than to Christ, saying, <hi type="italic">We have no king but Cæsar.</hi> Thus they thought to ingratiate themselves with their lords and masters. But for this God brought the Romans upon them, who <hi type="italic">took away their place and nation.</hi> 2. That he will not deliver them out of their hands: <hi type="italic">They shall smite the land,</hi> the whole land, and <hi type="italic">out of their hand I will not deliver them;</hi> and, if the Lord do not help them, none else can, nor can they help themselves. <div eID="gen20959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20960" type="x-p"/> III. A trial yet made whether their ruin might be prevented by sending Christ among them as a shepherd; God had sent his servants to them in vain, <hi type="italic">but last of all he sent unto them his Son, saying, They will reverence my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.37">Matt. xxi. 37</reference>. Divers of the prophets had spoken of him as the <hi type="italic">Shepherd of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Ezek. xxxiv. 23</reference>. He himself told the Pharisees that he was the <hi type="italic">Shepherd of the sheep,</hi> and that those who pretended to be shepherds were <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.1-John.10.2">John x. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.11">11</reference>), apparently referring to this passage, where we have, 1. The charge he received from his Father to try what might be done with this flock (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord my God</hi> (Christ called his Father <hi type="italic">his God</hi> because he acted in compliance with his will and with an eye to his glory in his whole undertaking), <hi type="italic">Feed the flock of the slaughter.</hi> The Jews were God's flock, but they were <hi type="italic">the flock of slaughter,</hi> for their enemies had killed them all the day long and <hi type="italic">accounted them as sheep for the slaughter;</hi> their own <hi type="italic">possessors slew them,</hi> and God himself had doomed them to the slaughter. Yet "<hi type="italic">feed them</hi> by reproof instruction, and comfort; provide wholesome food for those who have so long been soured with the leaven of the scribes and Pharisees." <hi type="italic">Other sheep he had, which were not of this fold,</hi> and which afterwards must be <hi type="italic">brought;</hi> but he is first <hi type="italic">sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.24">Matt. xv. 24</reference>. 2. His acceptance of this charge, and his undertaking pursuant to it, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">v. 7</reference>. He does as it were say, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come to do thy will, O my God!</hi> and, since this is thy will, it is mine: <hi type="italic">I will feed the flock of slaughter.</hi> Christ will care for these lost sheep; he will go about among them, <hi type="italic">teaching</hi> and <hi type="italic">healing even you, O poor of the flock!</hi> Christ did not neglect the meanest, nor overlook them for their meanness. The shepherds that made a prey of them regarded not the poor; they were conversant with those only that they could get by; but Christ preached his gospel <hi type="italic">to the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Matt. xi. 5</reference>. It was an instance of his humiliation that his converse was mostly with the inferior sort of people; his disciples, who were his constant attendants, were of the poor of the flock. 3. His furnishing himself with tools proper for the charge he had undertaken: I <hi type="italic">took unto me two staves,</hi> pastoral staves; other shepherds have but one crook, but Christ had two, denoting the double care he took of his flock, and what he did both for the souls and for the bodies of men. David speaks of God's <hi type="italic">rod</hi> and his <hi type="italic">staff</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Ps. xxiii. 4</reference>), a correcting rod and a supporting staff. One of these staves was called <hi type="italic">Beauty,</hi> denoting the temple, which is called <hi type="italic">the beauty of holiness</hi> and one of its gates <hi type="italic">beautiful,</hi> which Christ called his Father's house, and for which he showed a great zeal when he cleared it of the <hi type="italic">buyers and sellers;</hi> the other he called <hi type="italic">Bands,</hi> denoting their civil state, and the incorporate society of that nation, which Christ also took care of by preaching love and peace among them. Christ, in his gospel, and in all he did among them, consulted the advancement both of their civil and of their sacred interests. 4. His execution of his office, as the chief Shepherd. <hi type="italic">He fed the flock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">v. 7</reference>), and he displaced those under-shepherds that were false to their trust (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Three shepherds I cut off in one month.</hi> Through the deficiency and uncertainty of the history of the Jewish church, in its latter ages, we know not what particular event this had its accomplishment in; in general, it seems to be an act of power and justice for the punishment of the sinful shepherds and the redress of the grievances of the abused flock. Some understand it of the three orders of princes, priests, and scribes or prophets, who, when Christ had finished his work, were laid aside for their unfaithfulness. Others understand it of the three sects among the Jews, of Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herodians, all whom Christ silenced in dispute (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.1-Matt.22.46">Matt. xxii.</reference>) and soon after <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> all in a little time. <div eID="gen20960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20961" type="x-p"/> IV. Their enmity to Christ, and making themselves odious to him. He came to his own, the sheep of his own pasture; it might have been expected that between them and him there would be an entire affection, as between the shepherd and his sheep; but they conducted themselves so ill that <hi type="italic">his soul loathed them,</hi> was <hi type="italic">straitened</hi> towards them (so it may be read); he intended them kindness, but could not do them the kindness he intended them, <hi type="italic">because of their unbelief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.58">Matt. xiii. 58</reference>. He was disappointed in them, discouraged concerning them, <hi type="italic">grieved</hi> for them, not only for the shepherds, whom he cut off, but for the people, whom Christ often looked upon with grief in his heart and tears in his eyes. Their provocations even wore out his patience, and he was weary of that <hi type="italic">faithless and perverse generation. Their soul also it abhorred me;</hi> and therefore it was that his soul loathed them; for, whatever estrangement there is between God and man, it begins on man's side. The Jewish shepherds rejected this chief Shepherd, as the Jewish builders rejected this chief corner stone. They <hi type="italic">had indignation</hi> at Christ's doctrine and miracles, and his interest in the people, to whom they did all they could to render him odious, as they had made themselves odious to him. Note, There is a mutual enmity between God and wicked people; they are hateful to God and haters of God. Nothing speaks more the sinfulness and misery of an unregenerate state than this does. The carnal mind, the friendship of the world, are enmity to God, and God hates all the workers of iniquity; and it is easy to foresee what this will end in, if the quarrel be not taken up in time, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen20961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20962" type="x-p"/> V. Christ's rejecting them as incurable, and leaving them their house desolate, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>. The things of their peace are now hidden from their eyes, because they knew not the day of their visitation. Here we have, <div eID="gen20962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20963" type="x-p"/> 1. The sentence of their rejection passed (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then said I, I will not feed you.</hi> I will take no further care of you; <hi type="italic">you shall not see me again;</hi> take your own course. As I will not feed you, so I will not cure you; <hi type="italic">that that dieth, let it die</hi> (the Shepherd will do nothing to save its forfeited life); <hi type="italic">that that is to be cut off, let it be cut off;</hi> that which will make itself a prey to the wolf, let it be a prey, and let the rest so far forget their own mild and gentle nature as to <hi type="italic">eat the flesh of one another;</hi> let these sheep fight like dogs." Those that reject Christ will be certainly and justly rejected by him, and then are miserable of course. <div eID="gen20963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20964" type="x-p"/> 2. A sign of it given (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I took my staff, even Beauty, and cut it asunder,</hi> in token of this, that he would be no longer a shepherd to them, as the lord high steward determines his commission by breaking his white staff, and as Moses's breaking the tables of the law put a stop, for the present, to the treaty between God and Israel. The breaking of this staff signified the breaking of God's covenant which he had <hi type="italic">made with all the people,</hi> the covenant of peculiarity made with all the tribes of <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> and all other people who, by being proselyted to their religion, were incorporated into their nation. The Jewish church was now stripped of all its glory; its crown was profaned and cast to the ground, and all its honour laid in the dust; for God departed from it, and would no more own it for his. When Christ told them plainly that the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God</hi> should be <hi type="italic">taken from them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">given to another people,</hi> then be broke the <hi type="italic">staff of Beauty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Matt. xxi. 43</reference>. And <hi type="italic">it was broken in that day,</hi> though Jerusalem and the Jewish nation held up forty years longer, yet from that day we may reckon the staff of Beauty broken, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">v. 11</reference>. And though the great men did not, or would not, understand it as a divine sentence, but thought to put it by with a cold <hi type="italic">God forbid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.16">Luke xx. 16</reference>), yet the <hi type="italic">poor of the flock,</hi> the disciples of Christ, that <hi type="italic">waited on him,</hi> and understood with what authority he spoke, and could distinguish the voice of their Shepherd from that of a stranger, <hi type="italic">knew that it was the word of the Lord,</hi> and trembled at it, and were confident that it should not fall to the ground. Note, Christ is waited on by the poor of the flock; he chose them to be with him, to be his pupils, to be his witnesses; the poor received him and his gospel, when those that had great possessions turned their backs upon him. And those that wait upon Christ, that sit at his feet, to hear and receive his words, shall <hi type="italic">know of the doctrine whether it be of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen20964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20965" type="x-p"/> 3. A further reason given for their rejection. It was said before, <hi type="italic">Their souls abhorred him;</hi> and here we have an instance of it, their buying and selling him for thirty pieces of silver, either thirty Roman pence, or rather thirty Jewish shekels; this is here foretold in somewhat obscure expressions, as it is fit that such particular prophecies should be delivered, lest otherwise the plainness of the prophecy might prevent the accomplishment of it. Here, (1.) The Shepherd comes to them for his wages (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you think good, give me my price;</hi> you are weary of me, pay me off and discharge me; <hi type="italic">and, if not, forbear;</hi> if you be willing to continue me longer in your service, I will continue, or, if to turn me off without wages, I am content." Christ was no hireling, and yet the labourer is worthy of his hire. Compare with this what Christ said to Judas when he was going to sell him, "<hi type="italic">What thou doest do quickly;</hi> be at a word with the chief priests; let them either take the bargain or leave it," <reference osisRef="John.13.27">John xiii. 27</reference>. Those that betray Christ are not forced to it; they might have chosen. (2.) They value him at <hi type="italic">thirty pieces of silver.</hi> Many years' service he had done them as a Shepherd, yet this is all they will now turn him off with—"<hi type="italic">A goodly price that I</hi> with all my care and pains <hi type="italic">was valued at by them.</hi>" If Judas fixed this sum in his demand, it is observable that his name was <hi type="italic">Judah,</hi> the same name with that of the body of the people, for it was a national act; or, if (as it rather seems) the chief priests pitched upon this sum in their proffers, they were the representatives of the people; it was part of the priest's office to <hi type="italic">put a value</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">devoted things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.8">Lev. xxvii. 8</reference>), and thus they valued the Lord Jesus. It was the ordinary price of a slave, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Exod. xxi. 32</reference>. Making light of Christ, and undervaluing the love of that great and good Shepherd, are the ruin of multitudes, and justly so. (3.) The silver being no way proportionable to his worth, it is <hi type="italic">thrown to the potter</hi> with disdain: "Let him take it to buy clay with, or for any use that a little money will serve to, for it is not worth hoarding; it may be enough for a potter's stock, but not for the pay of such a shepherd, much less for his purchase." So the prophet <hi type="italic">cast the thirty pieces of silver to the potter in the house of the Lord:</hi> "Let him take them, and do what he will with them." Now we find a particular accomplishment of this in the history of Christ's sufferings, and reference is had to this prophecy, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.9-Matt.27.10">Matt. xxvii. 9, 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirty pieces of silver</hi> was the very sum for which Christ was sold to the chief priests; the money, when Judas would not keep it, and the chief priests would not take it back was laid out in the purchase of <hi type="italic">the potter's field.</hi> Even that sudden resolve of the chief priests was according to an ancient prophecy and the more ancient counsel and foreknowledge of God. <div eID="gen20965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20966" type="x-p"/> 4. The completing of their rejection in the cutting asunder of the other staff, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">v. 14</reference>. The former denoted the ruin of their church, by breaking the covenant between God and them—that defaced their <hi type="italic">beauty;</hi> this denotes the ruin of their state, by breaking the brotherhood between Judah and Israel, by reviving animosities and contention among them, such as were of old between Judah and Israel, the writing of whom as <hi type="italic">one stick in the hand of the Lord</hi> was one of the blessings promised after their return out of captivity, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.19">Ezek. xxxvii. 19</reference>. But that union shall now be dissolved; they shall be crumbled into parties and factions, exasperated one against another; and their kingdom, being thus divided, shall be <hi type="italic">brought to desolation.</hi> (1.) Nothing ruins a people so certainly, so inevitably, as the breaking of <hi type="italic">the staff of Bands,</hi> and the weakening of the brotherhood among them; for hereby they become an easy prey to the common enemy. (2.) This follows upon the dissolving of the covenant between God and them, and the decay of religion among them. When iniquity abounds love waxes cold. No wonder if those fall out among themselves that have provoked God to fall out with them. When the staff of Beauty is broken the staff of Bands will not hold long. An unchurched people will soon be an undone people.
entries.159eb4b35a81362ac6967953b75eabd94b59d26d: <div eID="gen20966" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted and Typified. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd. <hi type="super">16</hi> For, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken, nor feed that that standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces. <hi type="super">17</hi> Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened. <div eID="gen20967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20968" type="x-p"/> God, having shown the misery of this people in their being justly abandoned by the good Shepherd, here shows their further misery in being shamefully abused by a foolish shepherd. The prophet is himself to personate and represent this pretended shepherd (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take unto thee the instruments</hi> or accoutrements <hi type="italic">of a foolish shepherd,</hi> that are no way fit for the business, such a shepherd's coat, and bag, and staff, as a foolish shepherd would appear in; for such a shepherd shall be set over them (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.16">v. 16</reference>), who, instead of protecting them, shall oppress them and do them mischief. 1. They shall be under the inspection of unfaithful ministers. Their scribes, and priests, and doctors of their law, shall bind heavy burdens upon them, and grievous to be borne, and, with their traditions imposed, shall make the ceremonial law much more a yoke than God had made it. The description here given of the foolish shepherd suits very well with the character Christ gives of the scribes and Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.2">Matt. xxiii. 2</reference>. They shall be under the tyranny of unmerciful princes, that shall rule them with rigour, and make their own land as much a house of bondage to them as ever Egypt or Babylon was. When they had rejected him <hi type="italic">by whom princes decree justice</hi> it was just that they should be turned over to those who <hi type="italic">decree unrighteous decrees.</hi> 3. They shall be imposed upon and deluded by false Christs and false prophets, as our Saviour foretold, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Matt. xxiv. 5</reference>. Many such there were, who by their seditious practices provoked the Romans, and hastened the ruin of the Jewish nation; but it is observable that they were never cheated by a counterfeit Messiah till they had refused and rejected the true Messiah. Now observe, <div eID="gen20968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20969" type="x-p"/> I. What a curse this foolish shepherd should be to the people, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.16">v. 16</reference>. God will, for their punishment, <hi type="italic">raise up a</hi> foolish <hi type="italic">shepherd,</hi> who will not do the duty of a shepherd; he will not <hi type="italic">visit those that are cut off,</hi> nor go after those that go astray, nor seek those that are missing, to find them out and bring them home, as the good shepherd does, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.12-Matt.18.13">Matt. xviii. 12, 13</reference>. Their shepherds take no care of the <hi type="italic">young ones,</hi> that need their care and are well worthy of it, as Christ does, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>. They do not <hi type="italic">heal that</hi> which was <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> which was worried and torn, but let it die of its bruises, when a little thing, in time, would have saved it. They do not <hi type="italic">feed</hi> those who, through weakness, <hi type="italic">stand still,</hi> and are ready to faint, and cannot get forward, but leave them behind, let who will take them up; they do not <hi type="italic">carry</hi> that which <hi type="italic">stands still</hi> (so some read it); they never do any thing to <hi type="italic">support the weak</hi> and comfort the <hi type="italic">feeble-minded;</hi> but, on the contrary, 1. They are luxurious themselves: They <hi type="italic">eat of the flesh of the fat;</hi> they will have of the best for themselves; and, like that <hi type="italic">wicked servant</hi> that said, <hi type="italic">My lord delays his coming,</hi> they <hi type="italic">eat and drink with the drunken,</hi> and <hi type="italic">serve their own bellies.</hi> 2. They are barbarous to the flock. Their passions are as ill-governed as their appetites, for, when they are in a rage against any of the flock, they <hi type="italic">tear their</hi> very <hi type="italic">claws in pieces</hi> by over-driving them; they beat their hoofs; they <hi type="italic">smite their fellow servants. Woe unto thee, O land! when thy king is</hi> such <hi type="italic">a child!</hi> <div eID="gen20969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20970" type="x-p"/> II. What a curse this foolish shepherd should bring upon himself (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Woe to the idol-shepherd,</hi> who, like an idol, has eyes and sees not, who, like an idol, receives abundance of respect and homage from the people and the chief of their offerings, but neither can nor will do them any kindness. He <hi type="italic">leaves the flock</hi> when they most need his care, leaves them destitute, and flees, <hi type="italic">because he is a hireling;</hi> his doom is that <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> of God's justice shall be <hi type="italic">upon his arm</hi> and <hi type="italic">his right eye,</hi> so that he shall quite lose the use of both. <hi type="italic">His arm shall</hi> wither and <hi type="italic">be dried up,</hi> so that he who would not help his friends when it was required shall not know how to help himself; <hi type="italic">his right eye shall be utterly darkened,</hi> that he shall not discern the danger that his flock is in, nor know which way to look for relief. This was fulfilled when Christ said to the Pharisees, <hi type="italic">I have come that those who see may be made blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.39">John ix. 39</reference>. Those that have gifts which qualify them to do good, if they do not do good with them, shall be deprived of them; those that should have been workmen, but were slothful and would do nothing, will justly have their arm dried up; and those that should have been watchmen, but were sleepy and would never look about them, will justly have their eye blinded.  <chapter eID="Zech.11"/> <div eID="gen20970" type="x-p"/>

entries.96cb7a80fac516c86e63b8a815538580252c59fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13152"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.11.1-Zech.11.17">Zec 11:1-17</reference>. Destruction of the Second Temple and Jewish Polity for the Rejection of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen24793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13152"/><hi type="bold">1. Open thy doors, O Lebanon--</hi>that is, the temple so called, as being constructed of cedars of Lebanon, or as being lofty and conspicuous like that mountain (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">Ha 2:17</reference>). Forty years before the destruction of the temple, the tract called "Massecheth Joma" states, its doors of their own accord opened, and Rabbi Johanan in alarm said, I know that thy desolation is impending according to Zechariah's prophecy. Calvin supposes Lebanon to refer to Judea, described by its north boundary: "Lebanon," the route by which the Romans, according to Josephus, gradually advanced towards Jerusalem. Moore, from Hengstenberg, refers the passage to the civil war which caused the calling in of the Romans, who, like a storm sweeping through the land from Lebanon, deprived Judea of its independence. Thus the passage forms a fit introduction to the prediction as to Messiah born when Judea became a Roman province. But the weight of authority is for the former view. <div eID="gen24793" type="x-p"/>
entries.1531fbce2d884076efbffdc9ff2c5880117e8066: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13153"/><div sID="gen24794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13153"/><hi type="bold">2. fir tree ... cedar--</hi>if even the cedars (the highest in the state) are not spared, how much less the fir trees (the lowest)!<div eID="gen24794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest of ... vintage--</hi>As the vines are stripped of their grapes in the vintage (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>), so the forest of Lebanon "is come down," stripped of all its beauty. Rather, "the fortified" or "inaccessible forest" [Maurer]; that is, Jerusalem dense with houses as a thick forest is with trees, and "fortified" with a wall around. Compare <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>, where its desolate state is described as a forest. <div eID="gen24795" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a79b1b52c5d91cbca2c273b7bbed3fb9a053601: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13154"/><div sID="gen24796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13154"/><hi type="bold">3. shepherds--</hi>the Jewish rulers.<div eID="gen24796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their glory--</hi>their wealth and magnificence; or that of the temple, "their glory" (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">Mr 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.5">Lu 21:5</reference>).<div eID="gen24797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">young lions--</hi>the princes, so described on account of their cruel rapacity.<div eID="gen24798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pride of Jordan--</hi>its thickly wooded banks, the lair of "lions" (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jr 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">49:19</reference>). Image for Judea "spoiled" of the magnificence of its rulers ("the young lions"). The valley of the Jordan forms a deeper gash than any on the earth. The land at Lake Merom is on a level with the Mediterranean Sea; at the Sea of Tiberias it falls six hundred fifty feet below that level, and to double that depression at the Dead Sea, that is, in all, 1950 feet below the Mediterranean; in twenty miles' interval there is a fall of from three thousand to four thousand feet. <div eID="gen24799" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c9cff04191b11f3c41c202c0c66f42dc8badc32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13155"/><div sID="gen24800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13155"/>4. The prophet here proceeds to show the cause of the destruction just foretold, namely, the rejection of Messiah.<div eID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flock of ... slaughter--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">Psa 44:22</reference>). God's people doomed to slaughter by the Romans. Zechariah here represents typically Messiah, and performs in vision the actions enjoined: hence the language is in part appropriate to him, but mainly to the Antitype, Messiah. A million and a half perished in the Jewish war, and one million one hundred thousand at the fall of Jerusalem. "Feed" implies that the Jews could not plead ignorance of God's will to execute their sin. Zechariah and the other prophets had by God's appointment "fed" them (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>) with the word of God, teaching and warning them to escape from coming wrath by repentance: the type of Messiah, the chief Shepherd, who receives the commission of the Father, with whom He is one (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">Zec 11:4</reference>); and Himself says (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference>), "I will feed the flock of slaughter." Zechariah did not live to "feed" literally the "flock of slaughter"; Messiah alone "fed" those who, because of their rejection of Him, were condemned to slaughter. Jehovah-Messiah is the speaker. It is He who threatens to inflict the punishments (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.6">Zec 11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">8</reference>). The typical breaking of the staff, performed in vision by Zechariah (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">Zec 11:10</reference>), is fulfilled in His breaking the covenant with Judah. It is He who was sold for thirty pieces of silver (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen24801" type="x-p"/>
entries.72fadad699bfa404d0e904cd344b9ffdeac3e478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13156"/><div sID="gen24802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13156"/><hi type="bold">5. possessors--</hi>The buyers [Maurer], their Roman oppressors, contrasted with "they that sell men." The instruments of God's righteous judgment, and therefore "not holding themselves guilty" (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.7">Jr 50:7</reference>). It is meant that they might use this plea, not that they actually used it. Judah's adversaries felt no compunction in destroying them; and God in righteous wrath against Judah allowed it.<div eID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that sell them--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>). The rulers of Judah, who by their avaricious rapacity and selfishness (<reference osisRef="John.11.48">Joh 11:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.50">50</reference>) virtually sold their country to Rome. Their covetousness brought on Judea God's visitation by Rome. The climax of this was the sale of the innocent Messiah for thirty pieces of silver. They thought that Jesus was thus sold and their selfish interest secured by the delivery of Him to the Romans for crucifixion; but it was themselves and their country that they thus sold to the Roman possessors."<div eID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am rich--</hi>by selling the sheep (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.19">De 29:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Ho 12:8</reference>). In short-sighted selfishness they thought they had gained their object, covetous self-aggrandizement (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.14">Lu 16:14</reference>), and hypocritically "thanked" God for their wicked gain (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Lu 18:11</reference>).<div eID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say ... pity--</hi>In Hebrew it is singular: that is, each of those that sell them saith: Not one of their own shepherds pitieth them. An emphatical mode of expression by which each individual is represented as doing, or not doing, the action of the verb [Henderson]. Hengstenberg refers the singular verbs to Jehovah, the true actor; the wicked shepherds being His unconscious instruments. Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.6">Zec 11:6</reference>, For I will no more pity, with the Hebrew "pitieth not" here. <div eID="gen24805" type="x-p"/>
entries.38fdb7fdfbf068556cf8f4e6602a15cb509ea8bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13157"/><div sID="gen24806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13157"/>6. Jehovah, in vengeance for their rejection of Messiah, gave them over to intestine feuds and Roman rule. The Zealots and other factious Jews expelled and slew one another by turns at the last invasion by Rome.<div eID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his king--</hi>Vespasian or Titus: they themselves (<reference osisRef="John.19.15">Joh 19:15</reference>) had said, unconsciously realizing Zechariah's words, identifying Rome's king with Judah's ("his") king, "We have no king but Cæsar." God took them at their word, and gave them the Roman king, who "smote (literally, 'dashed in pieces') their land," breaking up their polity, when they rejected their true King who would have saved them. <div eID="gen24807" type="x-p"/>
entries.2272a8d891bb59701d174ff048865b66c59e96f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13158"/><div sID="gen24808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13158"/><hi type="bold">7. And--</hi>rather, "Accordingly": implying the motive cause which led Messiah to assume the office, namely, the will of the Father (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">Zec 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">5</reference>), who pitied the sheep without any true shepherd.<div eID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will feed--</hi>"I fed" [Calvin], which comes to the same thing, as the past tense must in Zechariah's time have referred to the event of Messiah's advent then future: the prophets often speaking of the future in vision as already present. It was not My fault, Jehovah implies, that these sheep were not fed; the fault rests solely with you, because ye rejected the grace of God [Calvin].<div eID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even you, O poor of the flock--</hi>rather, "in order that (I might feed, that is, save) the poor (humble; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">Zec 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.12">Zep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">Mt 5:3</reference>) of the flock"; literally, not you, but, "therefore (I will feed)" [Moore]. See Margin, "Verily the poor." It is for the sake of the believing remnant that Messiah took charge of the flock, though He would have saved all, if they would have come to Him. They would not come; therefore, as a nation, they are "the flock of (that is, doomed to) slaughter."<div eID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I took ... two staves--</hi>that is, shepherds' staves or rods (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). Symbolizing His assumption of the pastor's office.<div eID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beauty--</hi>The Jews' peculiar excellency above other nations (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">De 4:7</reference>), God's special manifestation to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.19">Psa 147:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">20</reference>), the glory of the temple ("the beauty of holiness," <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Psa 27:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">90:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>), the "pleasantness" of their land (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Ge 49:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">11:16</reference>), "the glorious land."<div eID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bands--</hi>implying the bond of "brotherhood" between Judah and Israel. "Bands," in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.61">Psa 119:61</reference>, Margin, is used for confederate companies: The Easterns in making a confederacy often tie a cord or band as a symbol of it, and untie it when they dissolve the confederacy [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Messiah would have joined Judah and Israel in the bonds of a common faith and common laws (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">Zec 11:14</reference>), but they would not; therefore in just retribution He broke "His covenant which He had made with all the people." Alexander, Antiochus Epiphanes, and Pompey were all kept from marring utterly the distinctive "beauty" and "brotherhood" of Judah and Israel, which subsisted more or less so long as the temple stood. But when Jehovah brake the staves, not even Titus could save the temple from his own Roman soldiery, nor was Jurian able to restore it. <div eID="gen24813" type="x-p"/>
entries.855f88fc985f7e684d1c7c011ea254f6bd1c555a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13159"/><div sID="gen24814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13159"/><hi type="bold">8. Three shepherds ... I cut off--</hi>literally, "to cause to disappear," to destroy so as not to leave a vestige of them. The three shepherds whom Messiah removes are John, Simon, and Eleazar, three leaders of factions in the Jewish war [Drusius]. Or, as Messiah, the Antitype, was at once prophet, priest, and king, so He by the destruction of the Jewish polity destroyed these three orders for the unbelief of both the rulers and people [Moore]. If they had accepted Messiah, they would have had all three combined in Him, and would have been themselves spiritually prophets, priests, and kings to God. Refusing Him, they lost all three, in every sense.<div eID="gen24814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one month--</hi>a brief and fixed space of time (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">Ho 5:7</reference>). Probably alluding to the last period of the siege of Jerusalem, when all authority within the city was at an end [Henderson].<div eID="gen24815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loathed them--</hi>literally, "was straitened" as to them; instead of being enlarged towards them in love (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.11">2Co 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">12</reference>). The same Hebrew as in <reference osisRef="Num.21.4">Nu 21:4</reference>, Margin. No room was left by them for the grace of God, as His favors were rejected [Calvin]. The mutual distaste that existed between the holy Messiah and the guilty Jews is implied. <div eID="gen24816" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5642979720c59d8641bd0ff8f4e8f9429882050: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13160"/><div sID="gen24817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13160"/><hi type="bold">9. Then said I--</hi>at last when all means of saving the nation had been used in vain (<reference osisRef="John.8.24">Joh 8:24</reference>).<div eID="gen24817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will not--</hi>that is, no more feed you. The last rejection of the Jews is foretold, of which the former under Nebuchadnezzar, similarly described, was the type (Jr 15:1-3; 34:17; 43:11; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>). Perish those who are doomed to perish, since they reject Him who would have saved them! Let them rush on to their own ruin, since they will have it so.<div eID="gen24818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat ... flesh of another--</hi>Let them madly perish by mutual discords. Josephus attests the fulfilment of this prophecy of threefold calamity: pestilence and famine ("dieth ... die"), war ("cut off ... cut off"), intestine discord ("eat ... one ... another"). <div eID="gen24819" type="x-p"/>
entries.d717f9660441381e8a8614444926d78ac250fbfd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13161"/><div sID="gen24820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13161"/><hi type="bold">10. covenant which I made with all the people--</hi>The covenant made with the whole nation is to hold good no more except to the elect remnant. This is the force of the clause, not as Maurer, and others translate. The covenant which I made with all the nations (not to hurt My elect people, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). But the Hebrew is the term for the elect people (Ammim), not that for the Gentile nations (Goiim). The Hebrew plural expresses the great numbers of the Israelite people formerly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20">1Ki 4:20</reference>). The article is, in the Hebrew, all the or those peoples. His cutting asunder the staff "Beauty," implies the setting aside of the outward symbols of the Jews distinguishing excellency above the Gentiles (see on <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference>) as God's own people. <div eID="gen24820" type="x-p"/>
entries.d99fb633c67ce83b7f43b8436f6bf2fbb9cf7e9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13162"/><div sID="gen24821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13162"/><hi type="bold">11. poor ... knew--</hi>The humble, godly remnant knew by the event the truth of the prediction and of Messiah's mission. He had, thirty-seven years before the fall of Jerusalem, forewarned His disciples when they should see the city compassed with armies, to "flee unto the mountains." Accordingly, Cestius Gallus, when advancing on Jerusalem, unaccountably withdrew for a brief space, giving Christians the opportunity of obeying Christ's words by fleeing to Pella.<div eID="gen24821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waited upon me--</hi>looked to the hand of God in all these calamities, not blindly shutting their eyes to the true cause of the visitation, as most of the nation still do, instead of referring it to their own rejection of Messiah. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.18-Isa.30.21">Is 30:18-21</reference> refers similarly to the Lord's return in mercy to the remnant that "wait for Him" and "cry" to Him (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.12">Zep 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen24822" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b986f4e2919ffa39068d69df48b95119c420321: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13163"/><div sID="gen24823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13163"/><hi type="bold">12. I said--</hi>The prophet here represents the person of Jehovah-Messiah.<div eID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If ye think good--</hi>literally, "If it be good in your eyes." Glancing at their self-sufficient pride in not deigning to give Him that return which His great love in coming down to them from heaven merited, namely, their love and obedience. "My price"; my reward for pastoral care, both during the whole of Israel's history from the Exodus, and especially the three and a half years of Messiah's ministry. He speaks as their "servant," which He was to them in order to fulfil the Father's will (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.7">Php 2:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if not, forbear--</hi>They withheld that which He sought as His only reward, their love; yet He will not force them, but leave His cause with God (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">5</reference>). Compare the type Jacob cheated of his wages by Laban, but leaving his cause in the hands of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.41">Ge 31:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">42</reference>).<div eID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">So ... thirty pieces of silver--</hi>thirty shekels. They not only refused Him His due, but added insult to injury by giving for Him the price of a gored bond-servant (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Ex 21:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.15">Mt 26:15</reference>). A freeman was rated at twice that sum. <div eID="gen24826" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3d5322322086ba855667db6dbb0a2c6a9666410: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13164"/><div sID="gen24827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13164"/><hi type="bold">13. Cast it unto the potter--</hi>proverbial: Throw it to the temple potter, the most suitable person to whom to cast the despicable sum, plying his trade as he did in the polluted valley (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Ki 23:10</reference>) of Hinnom, because it furnished him with the most suitable clay. This same valley, and the potter's shop, were made the scene of symbolic actions by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 18:1-19:15</reference>) when prophesying of this very period of Jewish history. Zechariah connects his prophecy here with the older one of Jeremiah: showing the further application of the same divine threat against his unfaithful people in their destruction under Rome, as before in that under Nebuchadnezzar. Hence <reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference>, in English Version, and in the oldest authorities, quotes Zechariah's words as Jeremiah's, the latter being the original author from whom Zechariah derived the groundwork of the prophecy. Compare the parallel case of <reference osisRef="Mark.1.2">Mr 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference> in the oldest manuscripts (though not in English Version), quoting Malachi's words as those of "Isaiah," the original source of the prophecy. Compare my Introduction to Zechariah. The "potter" is significant of God's absolute power over the clay framed by His own hands (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jr 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the house of the Lord--</hi>The thirty pieces are thrown down in the temple, as the house of Jehovah, the fit place for the money of Jehovah-Messiah being deposited, in the treasury, and the very place accordingly where Judas "cast them down." The thirty pieces were cast "to the potter," because it was to him they were "appointed by the Lord" ultimately to go, as a worthless price (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.6">Mt 27:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.10">7, 10</reference>). For "I took," "I threw," here Matthew has "they took," "they gave them"; because their (the Jews' and Judas') act was all His "appointment" (which Matthew also expresses), and therefore is here attributed to Him (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Ac 2:23</reference>; 4:28). It is curious that some old translators translate, for "to the potter," "to the treasury" (so Maurer), agreeing with <reference osisRef="Matt.27.6">Mt 27:6</reference>. But English Version agrees better with Hebrew and <reference osisRef="Matt.27.10">Mt 27:10</reference>. <div eID="gen24828" type="x-p"/>
entries.c497f79e6e07a2a484d6af61a6465b9d4da9d1a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13165"/><div sID="gen24829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13165"/>14. The breaking of the bond of union between Judah and Israel's ten tribes under Rehoboam is here the image used to represent the fratricidal discord of factions which raged within Jerusalem on the eve of its fall, while the Romans were thundering at its gates without. See Josephus [Wars of the Jews]. Also the continued severance of the tribes till their coming reunion (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">Ro 11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen24829" type="x-p"/>
entries.8df56c988b9243c56f0d38039485119fe6fe13e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13166"/><div sID="gen24830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13166"/><hi type="bold">15. yet--</hi>"take again"; as in <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference> previously he had taken other implements.<div eID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">instruments--</hi>the accoutrements, namely, the shepherd's crook and staff, wallet, &c. Assume the character of a bad ("foolish" in Scripture is synonymous with wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>) shepherd, as before thou assumedst that of a good shepherd. Since the Jews would not have Messiah, "the Good Shepherd" (<reference osisRef="John.10.11">Joh 10:11</reference>), they were given up to Rome, heathen and papal, both alike their persecutor, especially the latter, and shall be again to Antichrist, the "man of sin," the instrument of judgment by Christ's permission. Antichrist will first make a covenant with them as their ruler, but then will break it, and they shall feel the iron yoke of his tyranny as the false Messiah, because they rejected the light yoke of the true Messiah (Da 11:35-38; 12:<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">1; 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:3-12</reference>). But at last he is to perish utterly (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.17">Zec 11:17</reference>), and the elect remnant of Judah and Israel is to be saved gloriously. <div eID="gen24831" type="x-p"/>
entries.848084df01c0686f13af6d51881599e28a6200a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13167"/><div sID="gen24832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13167"/><hi type="bold">16. in the land--</hi>Antichrist will probably he a Jew, or at least one in Judea.<div eID="gen24832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not visit ... neither ... seek ... heal ... broken, nor feed ... but ... eat ... flesh ... tear--</hi>Compare similar language as to the unfaithful shepherds of Israel in <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2-Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:2-4</reference>. This implies, they shall be paid in kind. Such a shepherd in the worst type shall "tear" them for a limited time.<div eID="gen24833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those ... cut off--</hi>"those perishing" [Septuagint], that is, those sick unto death, as if already cut off.<div eID="gen24834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the young--</hi>The Hebrew is always used of human youths, who are really referred to under the image of the young of the flock. Ancient expositors [Chaldee Version, Jerome, &c.] translate, "the straying," "the dispersed"; so Gesenius.<div eID="gen24835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broken--</hi>the wounded.<div eID="gen24836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">standeth still--</hi>with faintness lagging behind.<div eID="gen24837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tear ... claws--</hi>expressing cruel voracity; tearing off the very hoofs (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.10.26">Ex 10:26</reference>), giving them excruciating pain, and disabling them from going in quest of pasture. <div eID="gen24838" type="x-p"/>
entries.98ecdac4d6c29a7a5fd1df19e2f8144705e33d8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13168"/><div sID="gen24839" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13168"/><hi type="bold">17. the idol--</hi>The Hebrew expresses both vanity and an idol. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.5">Re 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">6</reference>, as to the idolatrous and blasphemous claims of Antichrist. The "idol shepherd that leaveth the flock" cannot apply to Rome, but to some ruler among the Jews themselves, at first cajoling, then "leaving" them, nay, destroying them (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30-Dan.11.38">11:30-38</reference>). God's sword shall descend on his "arm," the instrument of his tyranny towards the sheep (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>); and on his "right eye," wherewith he ought to have watched the sheep (<reference osisRef="John.10.12">Joh 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.13">13</reference>). However, Antichrist shall destroy, rather than "leave the flock." Perhaps, therefore, the reference is to the shepherds who left the flock to Antichrist's rapacity, and who, in just retribution, shall feel his "sword" on their "arm," which ought to have protected the flock but did not, and on their "eye," which had failed duly to watch the sheep from hurt. The blinding of "the right eye" has attached to it the notion of ignominy (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1Sa 11:2</reference>). <chapter eID="Zech.11"/>

entries.6ac4de352d4986b3d142fed7c64237385b250a0d: <div eID="gen35681" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35682" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35683" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35683" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35682" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35684" type="x-p"/> The commencement of this chapter relates to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish polity, probably by the Babylonians; at least in the first instance, as the fourth verse speaks of the people thus threatened as the prophet's charge, <reference osisRef="Zac.11.1-Zac.11.6">Zac 11:1-6</reference>. The prophet then gives an account of the manner in which he discharged his office, and the little value that was put on his labors. And this he does by symbolical actions, a common mode of instruction with the ancient prophets, <reference osisRef="Zac.11.7-Zac.11.14">Zac 11:7-14</reference>. After the prophet, on account of the unsuccessfulness of his labors, had broken the two crooks which were the true badges of his pastoral office, (to denote the annulling of God's covenant with them, and their consequent divisions and dispersions), he is directed to take instruments calculated to hurt and destroy, perhaps an iron crook, scrip, and stones, to express by these symbols the judgments which God was about to inflict on them by wicked rulers and guides, who should first destroy the flock, and in the end be destroyed themselves, <reference osisRef="Zac.11.15-Zac.11.17">Zac 11:15-17</reference>. Let us now view this prophecy in another light, as we are authorized to do by Scripture, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.7">Mat 27:7</reference>. In this view the prophet, in the person of the Messiah, sets forth the ungrateful returns made to him by the Jews, when he undertook the office of shepherd in guiding and governing them; how they rejected him, and valued him and his labors at the mean and contemptible price of thirty pieces of silver, the paltry sum for which Judas betrayed him. Upon which he threatens to destroy their city and temple; and to give them up to the hands of such guides and governors as should have no regard to their welfare. <div eID="gen35684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35685" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35686" type="x-p"/> Open thy doors, O Lebanon - I will give Mr. Joseph Mede's note upon this verse: - "That which moveth me more than the rest, is in chap. 11, which contains a prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem, and a description of the wickedness of the inhabitants, for which God would give them to the sword, and have no more pity upon them. It is expounded of the destruction by Titus; but methinks such a prophecy was nothing seasonable for Zachary's time, (when the city yet for a great part lay in her ruins, and the temple had not yet recovered hers), nor agreeable to the scope. Zachary's commission, who, together with his colleague Haggai, was sent to encourage the people, lately returned from captivity, to build their temple, and to instaurate their commonwealth. Was this a fit time to foretell the destruction of both, while they were yet but a-building? And by Zachary too, who was to encourage them? Would not this better befit the desolation by Nebuchadnezzar?" I really think so. See Mr. J. Mede's 61. Epistle. <div eID="gen35686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35687" type="x-p"/> Lebanon signifies the temple, because built of materials principally brought from that place.
entries.4ba857c9b09b2fbd11a1f9aa8ea490d4735d2b5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35688" type="x-p"/> Howl, fir tree - This seems to point out the fall and destruction of all the mighty men.
entries.931d07e4a40fb661073be2775fbb3b0549a97bff: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35689" type="x-p"/> Young lions - Princes and rulers. By shepherds, kings or priests may be intended.
entries.c9d1f2113f4037134d00346e756c3941c169f6f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35690" type="x-p"/> Feed the flock of the slaughter - This people resemble a flock of sheep fattened for the shambles; feed, instruct, this people who are about to be slaughtered.
entries.4de6837fc6b4f878095d5166137be6de1df88017: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35691" type="x-p"/> Whose possessors - Governors and false prophets, slay them, by leading them to those things that will bring them to destruction. <div eID="gen35691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35692" type="x-p"/> And they that sell them - Give them up to idolatry; and bless God, strange to tell, that they get secular advantage by the establishment of this false religion.
entries.3818a5796364b6d8f18f5e0fbc603f606fab2938: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35693" type="x-p"/> For I will no more pity - I have determined to deliver them into the hands of the Chaldeans.
entries.d1e7f05408946032488a37e37ee05b5cccfcf6cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35694" type="x-p"/> And I wilt feed the flock of slaughter - I showed them what God had revealed to me relative to the evils coming upon the land; and I did this the more especially for the sake of the poor of the flock. <div eID="gen35694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35695" type="x-p"/> Two staves - Two shepherd's crooks. One I called Beauty - that probably by which they marked the sheep; dipping the end into vermillion, or some red liquid. And this was done when they were to mark every tenth sheep, as it came out of the field, when the tithe was to be set apart for the Lord. <div eID="gen35695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35696" type="x-p"/> The other I called Bands - Probably that with the hook or crook at the head of it, by which the shepherd was wont to catch the sheep by the horns or legs when he wished to bring any to hand. <div eID="gen35696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35697" type="x-p"/> And I fed the flock - These two rods show the beauty and union of the people, while under God as their Shepherd. It was the delight of God to see them in a state of peace and harmony.
entries.8d8b710a8436e19353290aebc8089eac69ec52ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35698" type="x-p"/> Three shepherds also I cut off in one month - Taking this literally, some think the three shepherds mean the three Maccabees, Judas, Jonathan, and Simon; others, the three wicked high priests, Jason, Alcimus, and Menelaus; others, the three last princes of the Asmonean race, Alexander, Hyrcanus, and Antigonus. <div eID="gen35698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35699" type="x-p"/> Perhaps three orders may be intended: <div eID="gen35699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35700" type="x-p"/> 1. The priesthood. <div eID="gen35700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35701" type="x-p"/> 2. The dictatorship, including the Scribes, Pharisees, etc. <div eID="gen35701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35702" type="x-p"/> 3. The magistracy, the great sanhedrin, and the smaller councils. <div eID="gen35702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35703" type="x-p"/> These were all annihilated by the Roman conquest.
entries.cef4a67dd11e068bcb3940834f34bc67e8193aba: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35704" type="x-p"/> I will not feed you - I shall instruct you no longer: some of you are appointed to death by famine; others, to be cut off by the sword; and others of you, to such desperation that ye shall destroy one another.
entries.03f8c5550c2e5dc84357bb8f3d150bdf5f7723ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35705" type="x-p"/> I took my staff - Beauty, and cut it asunder - And thus I showed that I determined no longer to preserve them in their free and glorious state. And thus I brake my covenant with them, which they had broken on their part already.
entries.5e251c44d5f4c667863bc7c49af23fe23aee00ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35706" type="x-p"/> So the poor of the flock - The pious, who attended to my teaching, saw that this was the word - the design, of God.
entries.70bdbb5a1de6f2c827b45042febb406137044afc: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35707" type="x-p"/> If ye think good, give me my price - "Give me my hire." And we find they rated it contemptuously; thirty pieces of silver being the price of a slave, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.32">Exo 21:32</reference>.
entries.8bc283ef4618551f21639c944bda1a15c639f0ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35708" type="x-p"/> And the Lord said unto me, Cast it unto the potter - Jehovah calls the price of his prophet his own price; and commands that it should not be accepted, but given to a potter, to foreshadow the transaction related <reference osisRef="Mat.27.7">Mat 27:7</reference>. "Earthen vessels were used in the temple; and we may suppose that some Levites were employed within the sacred precincts to furnish them. To these, the humblest of his ministers in the temple, God commands that the degrading price should be cast." This is the substance of the notes on these two verses, given by Abp. Newcome. <div eID="gen35708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35709" type="x-p"/> We may look at it in another light, Give me my price! הבו שכרי habu sichri, bring my price, or give him any price; that is, Give the money to Judas which you have agreed to give him; for he can neither betray me nor you crucify me, but my own permission. But if not, forbear; take time to consider this bloody business, and in time forbear. For though I permit you to do it, yet remember that the permission does not necessitate you to do it; and the salvation of the world may be effected without this treachery and murder. <div eID="gen35709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35710" type="x-p"/> See my notes on this place, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.9">Mat 27:9</reference>, where I have examined the evidence for the reading of "Zechariah the prophet," instead of "Jeremiah."
entries.3e0ec8b7d4392a0714e07d28e07436f4b305aeb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35711" type="x-p"/> That I might break the brotherhood - I cannot, says Newcome, explain this passage, without supposing that the kingdom of Israel subsisted when the prophet wrote it; and that either the wars between Judah and Israel are referred to, (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.5">2Kgs 16:5</reference>), or the captivity of the ten tribes, when the brotherly connection between these kingdoms ceased.
